narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 69% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking in your third year of law school was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) placed you well below the average student who was accepted, who typically ranked around the middle of their class. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle to pass the bar.

Your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA also mattered, but they worked in the opposite direction. Both scores were slightly below the average of accepted students (35 versus 37 for the LSAT and 2.7 versus 3.23 for GPA), yet they still provided a modest push toward predicting that you would pass. Unfortunately, these positive signals were not strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your third-year class ranking.

Your first-year ranking (decile 4 versus an average of 6) and middle family income also played smaller roles but did not change the overall outlook.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT if possible. Building a stronger record in your remaining law school work or gaining targeted bar-prep experience could help demonstrate your readiness for future applications.
